SeeGenesis 16:1–3. Sarah’s offering of her servant Hagar to Abraham followed ancient customs in cases of infertility (see Camille Fronk Olson, “The Matriarchs: Administrators of God’s Covenantal Blessings,” in Belnap and Schade,From Creation to Sinai, 392–93).

Jacob 2:30. Regarding Abraham’s plural marriage to Hagar, the Lord said, “God commanded Abraham, and Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham to wife. And why did she do it? Because this was the law; and from Hagar sprang many people. This, therefore, was fulfilling, among other things, the promises” (Doctrine and Covenants 132:34).
See Gospel Topics Essays, “Plural Marriage in The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints,” Gospel Library.
Gospel Topics Essays, “Plural Marriage in Kirtland and Nauvoo,” Gospel Library.

The Hebrew word used to describe Hagar’s attitude toward Sarah indicates that Sarah became small or insignificant in Hagar’s eyes or that Hagar treated Sarah with contempt (see Longman and Strauss,The Baker Expository Dictionary, entry 7043, page 1014).
SeeRomans 3:23–26;2 Nephi 2:8. See also Avram R. Shannon, “Abraham: A Man of Relationships,” in Belnap and Schade,From Creation to Sinai, 295‒99.
Doctrine and Covenants 84:14. See also History, 1838–1856 (Manuscript History of the Church), volume E-1,1708,josephsmithpapers.org.

Even though Hagar was acting as surrogate for Sarah, the Lord revealed to Hagar what Ishmael’s name would be, along with the promise that her seed would be multiplied (seeGenesis 16:10–14). Hagar is one of only a handful of women in scripture who received a divine annunciation of the birth of her own child (seeGenesis 16:10–12; see alsoJudges 13:2–5;1 Samuel 1:17, 19–20;Luke 1:26–38). Only Hagar and Mary were told what to name their sons.
Topics and Questions, “Abraham, Book of,” Gospel Library.

Some have speculated that Pharaoh did not have the right to the priesthood because he was a descendant of Cain through Egyptus, the wife of Ham. But this view goes beyond what the scriptures teach and should not be perpetuated today.
